trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.
Going up would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going down would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes right.
Number 2 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
I can't rule out right or down yet, so I'll make an educated guess: right.

Going around the edge to (5,1) would force the line onto number 8 before its turn; going left would leave number 4 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes around the edge to (1,5).

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going around the edge to (1,1), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves; going down, the next 3 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at number 5. So my guess (right from number 2) was wrong, so the line must go down.
Number 3 is next and right here, so the line takes it.

Going around the edge to (1,5) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order); going around the edge to (5,1) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes up.
Number 4 is next and right here, so the line takes it.

Going around the edge to (3,1) would force the line onto number 8 before its turn; going up would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes left.
Number 5 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going left would force the line onto number 7 before its turn. So the line goes right.
I can't rule out around the edge to (2,1) or up yet, so I'll make an educated guess: around the edge to (2,1).
Going down would force the line onto number 8 before its turn; going up leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes right.
Going down would leave both cell (3,1) and number 7 needing the line next, and it can't do both; going up leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes right.
Going up would force the line onto number 9 before its turn. So the line goes down.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes left.
Going around the edge to (1,1) leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes right.
Going around the edge to (1,2) would strand number 9: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes right.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes around the edge to (1,3).
Every cell is covered and the numbers are in order. Case closed!
I grow a search tree: my policy network suggests moves, a trained value head judge them. 40 simulations per move.
One of my simulated futures reached the end after 15 simulations. Following it!
Let evolution do the work: 24 random lines compete, the fittest breed and mutate.
Generation 0: the best random line covers 20/25 cells (80%).
Generation 1: fitness 25/25. The best line covers 25 cells.
Generation 1: a perfect line evolved! Every cell covered.
Feeling lucky! Before every move I'll play 24 random futures and bet on the move that survives most often.
Jackpot! A future after going right covers the whole board. Cashing in!
Let x(cell, step) mean 'this cell is step number <step> of the line'. 25 cells x 25 steps, minus everything that's impossible at a glance.
Encoded 1,450 variables and 3,947 clauses in 0.00 s (428 position variables survive the pruning).
Solver found a model in 0.00 s. Decoding it into a line...
Q.E.D. Every clause is satisfied.
